records.name: Masovian Voivodeship
records.summary:
Masovian, anchored by Warsaw, is the institutional counterweight to Poland's eastern resolution belt. On 6 February 2024, Warsaw's Voivodeship Administrative Court repealed the last remaining "against LGBT ideology" document in the country. Warsaw is the origin point of the progressive response: in February 2019 Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski signed a 12-point LGBT+ Declaration (security, education, culture, sport, employment; drawn up with LGBT NGOs, including an intervention hostel and school "lighthouse keeper" projects), which provoked the first anti-LGBT municipal resolution (Świdnik, March 2019) as an explicit counter-reaction. The administrative-court campaign, led from Warsaw by the national Commissioner for Human Rights and carried through the provincial administrative courts and the Supreme Administrative Court, dismantled the resolution network nationally.

The unit's dark stain is historical: in May 2005 the city under mayor Lech Kaczyński banned that year's Parada Równości, and the ECtHR in Bączkowski and Others v. Poland (2007) ruled the ban violated Articles 11, 13, and 14 ECHR. This is 20 years past and has not been repeated; the current institutional trajectory is clearly positive.

Score of 0.56 sits 0.04 above the national 0.52. The only unit scoring above national in this dossier; well above Małopolska (0.48) and the eastern belt (0.42–0.45), where the resolution legacy dominates and no equivalent court-repeal or declaration infrastructure exists.

freshness.fact: Warsaw's 2019 LGBT+ Declaration shows no record of repeal; Warsaw remains the most LGBT-friendly major Polish city; no reversal found in searches.
As of 24 Apr 2025 every anti-LGBT resolution and Family Charter in Poland is withdrawn or court-invalidated; the article itself now documents a completed episode.
2007 ECtHR judgment remains binding precedent on assembly bans; Polish courts applied the line of cases through the 2019-2024 ban reversals.

records.name: Bauchi
records.summary:
Bauchi sits in the twelve-state Sharia criminal bloc of northern Nigeria, and it is where that system's ultimate penalty was actually pronounced: in June 2022 a Sharia court in Ningi sentenced three men — including a 70-year-old — to death by stoning for same-sex acts after arrest by the Hisbah religious police, reportedly the first time a death sentence has actually been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria. The sentence was pronounced, not carried out; no execution is on record.

The appellate counterweight is real but fragile: the state's Upper Sharia Court quashed two stoning death sentences in 2003 (denial of counsel, defective confession), and Amnesty International recorded a string of similar successful appeals. A June 2025 country-of-origin note confirms the code remains in force, and corporal enforcement of Sharia morality law in Bauchi continues to be cited in 2025–26 advisory material.

freshness.fact: The July 2022 Bauchi stoning sentences did not stand: accused were released on bail pending appeal and no execution has occurred; sharia capital exposure nonetheless remains live (Aug 2026 UK advisory; 2025 Akwa Ibom case).

freshness.fact: Historical baseline (2004): sharia criminal provisions in Bauchi then and now carry severe/symbolic-punishment exposure; provisions unchanged, though 2022-26 cases show appellate friction.
Incident record (2014 floggings) unchallenged; corporal enforcement of sharia morality law in Bauchi continues to be cited in 2026 advisory context.

records.name: Kano
records.summary:
Kano is one of twelve northern Nigerian states running a parallel Sharia criminal code for Muslims: its Penal Code Law took effect 26 November 2000, prescribing 100 lashes plus up to a year's imprisonment for unmarried persons convicted of consensual same-sex activity and stoning to death for married or previously-married offenders. The state's Hisbah religious police are documented as the most active command among the three states studied in a 2019 rights-monitoring survey of 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 — enforcement that operates alongside, not merely on paper beside, the secular police.

A June 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms the Sharia codes remain in force and singles out Kano as one of only two states whose law carries a capital maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as men. No trans-specific incident is on the state's record; the capital text plus the most active morality-police infrastructure is the finding.

freshness.fact: Kano's Sharia provisions remain in force (death by stoning for men, liti for women); a Sharia court death sentence (reported Jul 2022, Reuters) and 2024 arrest waves confirm live application.

freshness.fact: Equaldex current-version entry (2024): homosexual activity in Kano illegal, death penalty as punishment, in force since Nov 2000; no change found since.
Sharia codes in force in Kano (named); death maximum for liwat; Kano one of two states where lesbianism also carries maximum death penalty.

records.name: Sokoto
records.summary:
Sokoto's Sharia Penal Code took effect 31 January 2001 within Nigeria's twelve-state religious-criminal bloc: male same-sex activity draws stoning to death for married or previously-married offenders and 100 lashes for the unmarried, and acts between women are punished by discretionary sentence of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment. A 2019 rights-monitoring study of 173 Sharia-court cases (2017) covers Sokoto among the three sample states, confirming operational religious courts and Hisbah activity there, and a June 2025 government note confirms the codes remain in force.

No capital sentence is on record as imposed in Sokoto — that record belongs to a neighbouring state — and no trans-specific incident is documented. The finding is capital-heavy statutory text combined with verified court-level enforcement.

records.name: Yobe
records.summary:
Yobe is one of the twelve northern Nigerian states that extended religious law into criminal jurisdiction during the 1999–2002 wave, giving Sharia courts authority over Muslims for conduct beyond the federal criminal code. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms the Sharia penal codes in these states — Yobe among them — remain in force, with the death penalty as the maximum for men's same-sex acts across all twelve and penalties for women ranging up to death in a minority of states; the same note's enforcement section records the 2023 public flogging of a person for cross-dressing, a trans-adjacent Sharia-police punishment.

Yobe's own dossier records no state-level court-case study and no further named incidents; the risk profile is the parallel criminal jurisdiction itself plus bloc-wide enforcement reporting, set against federal law that reaches only men's acts.

records.name: Zamfara
records.summary:
Zamfara is where Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave began: its governor introduced the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, and by 2002 eleven more northern states followed — a parallel system of Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, which the 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms is still operative and capital-punishment-capable for same-sex acts. A 2019 rights-monitoring study of 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 uses Zamfara as one of three sample states, confirming the courts function in practice, not just on paper.

No capital sentence is on record as imposed in Zamfara, and no trans-specific incident appears in the dossier; the finding is pioneering the bloc's enforcement architecture and hosting functioning religious courts.

records.name: Borno
records.summary:
Borno is one of the twelve northern Nigerian states applying Sharia criminal law in parallel with the federal system since the 1999–2002 wave. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note lists Borno among the states where the Sharia penal code remains in force for Muslims, criminalising same-sex acts between men (death penalty the maximum) and between women (penalties up to flogging and imprisonment), with a dedicated section on enforcement and the religious police — the legal architecture, not a case record, is the finding.

No trans-specific incident, no Hisbah case and no court-level study covers Borno in this dossier; the bloc's own reporting caveat is that enforcement data capture only a fraction of actual cases, so silence is not evidence of safety. The federal criminal code's coverage of men's acts (up to 14 years) applies here as everywhere in Nigeria.

freshness.fact: Historical record of 2000-04 hisbah/sharia excesses in Borno; Borno's sharia criminal code remains in force, so the pattern remains relevant background.
UK CPIN on Nigeria SOGI is the freshest consolidated source (asset ID indicates 2025 update); confirms SSMPA + northern sharia statutes in force incl. Borno.
Sharia penal code remains in force for Muslims in Borno; death is maximum penalty for men for liwat (sodomy); CPIN lists Borno among northern states with sharia codes in force.

records.name: Gombe
records.summary:
Gombe applies Sharia criminal law as part of the twelve-state northern bloc adopted by 2002. The Sharia layer criminalises conduct beyond the federal SSMPA, including same-sex acts between women; the framework applies to Muslims, and its practical reach over visitors is mediated by arrest practice - including hisbah morality policing in the northern block - rather than by any formal 'tourists excepted' rule. No trans-specific incident or documented Hisbah activity appears in this dossier for Gombe. Reporting-decay caveats apply: absence of records reflects fear of outing and surveillance gaps, not absence of risk.

Score 0.024 below the national 0.08. Tied with the generic-Sharia tier (Borno, Jigawa, Kaduna, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger): the enacted parallel criminal system is the deviation, without additional case-level or enforcement evidence to push further. Well above Kano (0.03) and Bauchi (0.02), which have death-penalty text or carried-out capital sentences respectively.

freshness.fact: Same-sex conduct remains criminalised in Gombe under the Sharia penal provisions; the 2004-era baseline was tightened nationally by the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (up to 14 years), still in force.
Current authoritative source: FCDO country policy note on SOGIE in Nigeria, last modified 25 Jun 2025; describes continuing criminalisation and extortion-based enforcement.

Criminalisation in force (sharia group states). Gombe Oct-2023 mass arrest: 23 people still detained a month later, risks of 'rehabilitation centre' conversion practices, per Human Dignity Trust profile quoted in CPIN.
